Security skills

Three skills that keep bad practice out of the code and out of the release: secrets in the repo, missing object-level authorization, unvalidated input, containers running as root, services shipping without a tested rollback.

Take them, adapt them, share them Every control anchored to a standard you can download Not in the plugin, on purpose

What they are anchored to

Nothing here depends on a private policy, a named vendor, or a document you cannot obtain.

AnchorUsed for
OWASP ASVS v5.0The requirement set, and the L1 / L2 / L3 assurance ladder
OWASP Top 10:2025 · API Security Top 10 2023 · CWE Top 25Naming a defect precisely enough to test for it
NIST SP 800-63B · SP 800-218 (SSDF) · SP 800-218AAuthentication assurance; lifecycle practices; the generative-AI profile
CIS Docker Benchmark · NIST SP 800-190Container build and runtime hardening
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025The AI / agent / MCP overlay
CVSS v4.0 · EPSS · CISA KEVThe vulnerability gate

Two things follow from that, and both are improvements

A client can verify the work. Every threshold is either cited or explicitly labelled a T-Gency default they are free to replace with their own policy — secret rotation cadence, log retention, remediation SLAs, exception approval levels.

The gaps become visible. An earlier version of these skills silently omitted CSRF, SSRF, object-level authorization, insecure deserialization, CORS, mass assignment, password hashing, JWT validation, SBOM and signing — several of which sit in the current OWASP and CWE top tens. They are covered here.

The sentence worth saying out loud in a client room: these are our defaults; if you have a policy, we run against yours.

The three skills

SkillUse it when
secure-devWriting or reviewing application code. Threat modelling, authentication, authorization (including object- and property-level), sessions, injection and output encoding, CSRF / SSRF / CORS, cryptography, secret handling, error handling, rate limiting, security logging, supply chain, and the AI / agent / MCP overlay
secure-container-imagesAnything with a Dockerfile or Containerfile. Multi-stage builds, non-root, capabilities, read-only root filesystem, image scanning, SBOM and signing
production-readiness-gateDeciding whether something ships. A six-pillar go/no-go with a vulnerability gate, graded on evidence found in the repository

What the gate is, precisely

An engineering assessment — not a compliance certification and not an approval authority. A GO means the controls we could check are implemented and evidenced in this repository at this commit. It does not replace a penetration test, an architecture review, a compliance audit, or the accountable owner's sign-off.

When a client asks whether it helps with an audit programme, the honest answer is that it produces engineering evidence their compliance function can evaluate as one input, and that whether it satisfies any given control is their determination.

The orientation mapping in production-readiness-gate/references/standards-mapping.md exists for exactly that conversation, and carries the same caveat at the top of the file. It deliberately omits SOC 2: the Trust Services Criteria are an AICPA framework assessed by a licensed CPA firm over a defined period, and claiming an engineering tool maps onto one creates contractual exposure for whoever makes the claim.

Three rules that make the output worth reading

These are the parts most likely to be lost when someone adapts the skills, and the parts that matter most:

  • A PASS without a citation is an UNVERIFIED. Cite a file and a line, a pipeline step, or a document reference — or do not claim it
  • Never report "could not check" as "not present". They lead to different actions: one means build it, the other means show me it exists
  • A gate failure is evidence of a gap; a gate pass is not evidence of an implementation. Half the container controls are runtime settings a Dockerfile review cannot observe at all

Classification, and the ASVS level it selects

Two steps, deliberately separate, so the scheme is portable.

Classification is T-Gency's scoping matrix — three variables any team can assess in a meeting: data handled (Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted), availability and integrity impact (Low / High), and exposure (internet-facing / internal only). The verification level is OWASP ASVS, so a client's auditor, a pentester or a new engineer can check the work against something they can download.

TypeASVS levelWhy
P1, I1L1ASVS L1 is the floor for every application. There is no tier below it
P2L1 + L2 on V13 Configuration, V16 LoggingPublic data, but an outage or defacement is material
I2, C1L2Data whose loss materially hurts the business
C2, R1L2 + L3 on V8 Authorization, V11 Cryptography, V14 Data ProtectionThe data path earns L3 even when access is internal only
R2L3Highest sensitivity and highest impact

When in doubt, classify up. The cost of over-classifying is some extra verification work; the cost of under-classifying is discovering the gap in production. And classify by the most sensitive data the system can reach, not by the data on the happy path — a dashboard that renders public metrics but holds a credential that can read the customer table is classified on the customer table.

The two rows worth arguing about in the room

The team says…TypeASVSAI overlay
"A support chatbot over our public FAQ"P1L1✓
"An agent that reads customer tickets and issues refunds"R2L3✓

The chatbot is genuinely low risk — until someone connects it to a tool. The refund agent is a payments system that happens to have a model in front of it, and classifying it as anything less is the mistake this table exists to prevent.

Where they run in the delivery loop

Not at the end. Three touchpoints, and the first is the one that matters.

WhenWhichWhy
Writing the Specsecure-dev, starting with the threat modelSo NFR-* and TC-* come from a real control list and a real threat list, not from intuition. Security shapes the WHAT
Phase 2, completenesssecure-dev, secure-container-imagesImplementing the constraints the Spec already committed to. Nothing new is discovered here
Before the PRproduction-readiness-gateThe go/no-go over the complete feature, on evidence

Running only the last one turns security into a veto at the most expensive moment, and the one most likely to get waived under deadline.

The one principle behind the AI overlay

The model is an untrusted component sitting inside your trust boundary.

Not malicious — untrusted, in the precise sense: its output is a function of inputs you do not fully control, and it can be steered by anyone who can get text in front of it. A document it summarises, a web page it reads, a tool result, a field in a database row.

Every control in the overlay follows from that. If you find yourself reasoning "the model wouldn't do that", stop: you are relying on a prompt as a security boundary. There is no reliable filter for prompt injection — so design so that a successful injection cannot cause harm, rather than trying to prevent every injection.

Invoking them

Plain language. You never type a skill's name:

  • Is this endpoint secure? Review it against our standards.
  • Review this Dockerfile for security issues.
  • Is this service ready for production?

The description in each SKILL.md is what routes the request. If you adapt a skill and it stops loading when you expect it to, the description is where to look — not the instructions.

Adapting them for a client

  1. Replace the classification if they have one. secure-dev/references/solution-typology.md separates the P1–R2 scoping matrix from the ASVS level it selects, precisely so the first half can be swapped for the client's data-classification scheme while the controls stay anchored to a public standard
  2. Replace every T-Gency default with their policy where they have one. Each is labelled as a default in the text. Record which policy and which version you assessed against
  3. Keep the evidence rules — the three in the box above. They are what make the output worth reading
  4. Say what you did not assess. Every report shape here has a section for it. It is not optional: a report that is silent about its blind spots reads as a clean bill of health it has not earned

Installing them

mkdir -p .claude/skills
cp -r skills/secure-dev skills/secure-container-images skills/production-readiness-gate .claude/skills/

Or package them as a plugin if you want a version number and one install command for a team — section 5 covers the manifest shape.

Known gaps

Stated rather than implied, because a checklist that hides its edges is worse than a short one.

  • Infrastructure as code and Kubernetes beyond the container security context: no Terraform, NetworkPolicy, cluster RBAC or admission-policy coverage
  • Mobile and desktop clients: none
  • Model safety and evaluation — whether a model produces harmful output — as opposed to the security of the system around the model
  • Privacy engineering beyond data minimisation and retention: no data mapping, subject-rights workflow, or international transfer analysis
  • Cloud provider configuration: IAM policy, network architecture and storage permissions are assessed only where they appear as code in the repository

Multi-tenant row-level security used to be on this list. It is now covered in secure-dev §3.2, which requires the tenant predicate to be enforced in the data layer and a test that proves a cross-tenant read fails.

Check what else is missing for your stack before assuming the list is complete.
